description: A first course in financial accounting that assumes nothing. You learn the double-entry system, record and verify transactions, make the adjustments that real books need, prepare final accounts for a trader and for a non-profit, handle bills of exchange, consignment and joint ventures, and finish by reading financial statements the way a lender or investor does. Every unit has worked examples with checked numbers, a short case study, practice questions and a unit test.

lessons.title: What accounting is, who uses it and why
objectives: Define accounting and distinguish it from book-keeping
Name the main users of financial statements and what each one wants to know
Distinguish financial, cost and management accounting

blocks.text: The process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating the financial transactions of an organisation so that users can take informed decisions.

Book-keeping is the clerical part: noting every transaction in the right book. Accounting begins where book-keeping stops. It classifies those entries, summarises them into statements, and interprets the result. A shop assistant who enters bills in a register is book-keeping. The person who tells the owner that credit sales are growing faster than collections is accounting.

Why bother? Because memory fails and owners cheat themselves. Without records you cannot say how much profit the business made, how much customers owe you, how much you owe suppliers, or whether the bank loan can be repaid. Law also requires it: the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company to keep proper books of account, and the Income-tax Act and GST law require records from any business above their thresholds.

blocks.caption: Who uses accounting information
rows: Did I earn a profit and can I withdraw money?
Profit and loss account, drawings, capital
Can this business repay my loan with interest?
Cash flow, current ratio, debt-equity ratio
Will I be paid on credit terms?
Is the business growing and is it worth its price?
Can the firm afford wage increases and is my job safe?
Is tax computed correctly on the true income?
Books for income tax and GST returns
Will this firm still exist to honour warranties?

blocks.text: Accounting has three main branches. Financial accounting records historical transactions and reports to outsiders through standard statements. Cost accounting works out what each product or service costs to make. Management accounting uses both to help managers plan and control. This course is about financial accounting; the other two build on it in later semesters.

A kirana store and a listed company use the same double-entry logic. What differs is the rulebook: a sole proprietor mainly follows the Income-tax Act and the GST Acts, while a company must follow the Companies Act, 2013 and the accounting standards notified under it.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a function of accounting rather than book-keeping?
options: Preparing the balance sheet and interpreting it
Entering a sale in the sales register
Posting a journal entry to the ledger
mcq.explain: Summarising and interpreting are accounting functions. Recording and posting are book-keeping.

mcq.q: A bank deciding whether to grant a loan is mainly interested in the business's
mcq.explain: Lenders look at repayment capacity: cash flows, liquidity and solvency.

short.q: Distinguish between book-keeping and accounting. Give one example of each.
short.model_answer: Book-keeping is the systematic recording of transactions, for example entering a credit sale in the sales book. Accounting includes classifying and summarising those records and interpreting the results, for example preparing the profit and loss account and explaining why profit fell. Book-keeping is routine and clerical; accounting needs judgement and produces information for decisions.

common_mistakes: Treating accounting as only a tax chore. Its first customer is the owner.
Writing 'accounting is the language of business' with no explanation. Say what it communicates and to whom.
lessons.exam_tip: For a 5-mark definition question write the definition, name the stages (identify, measure, record, classify, summarise, communicate) and add one line on users. Three parts get full marks.

lessons.title: Accounting concepts, conventions and the standards framework
objectives: State and apply the basic accounting concepts and conventions
Explain why accounting rules are standardised
Outline the Indian framework: Accounting Standards (AS), Ind AS, ICAI, MCA and NFRA

blocks.text: If every accountant were free to measure things differently, two businesses could not be compared and no lender would trust a balance sheet. The profession therefore works to a shared set of rules called Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, or GAAP. In India GAAP means the Companies Act, 2013, the accounting standards notified under it, and accepted accounting practice.

blocks.caption: Basic accounting concepts
rows: The business is separate from its owner
Rohan's personal grocery bill is not a business expense
Only transactions measurable in money are recorded
The skill of a manager is not an asset in the books
The business will continue for the foreseeable future
Machinery is valued at cost less depreciation, not at scrap value
Profit is reported for a fixed period, usually a year
Indian businesses use 1 April to 31 March
Assets are recorded at purchase cost
Land bought for 20 lakh stays at 20 lakh even if it is now worth 50 lakh
Every transaction has two equal effects
Buying furniture for cash raises furniture and lowers cash
Revenue is recognised when it is earned, not when advance is received
An order is not a sale until goods are delivered
Record income and expense when they arise, not when cash moves
March rent paid in April belongs to March
Charge the expenses of a period against the revenue of that same period
Cost of goods sold sits in the same year as the sale

blocks.caption: Accounting conventions
rows: Use the same methods year after year so results can be compared
Provide for all expected losses, do not anticipate profits
Record items that could change a decision; ignore trivial ones
Statements must reveal everything that a user needs to know

blocks.text: Accounting standards turn these ideas into detailed rules. In India they are issued in two layers. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) recommends standards; the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) notifies them under the Companies Act. Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards) are converged with IFRS and apply to listed companies and to unlisted companies with net worth of 250 crore rupees or more, along with their holding, subsidiary and associate companies. Smaller companies follow the older Accounting Standards (AS). The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) oversees the quality of audit and compliance for larger companies.
A sole proprietor is not bound by the Companies Act, but the concepts above still apply, and the Income-tax Act expects the books to follow a consistent method of accounting.
Conservatism is the concept students misuse most. It means do not overstate profit or assets. It does not mean deliberately hide profit; hidden reserves are a violation of true and fair presentation.

mcq.q: Purchase of a machine for 5,00,000 is recorded at that amount even if its market value rises to 7,00,000 next year. Which concept applies?
mcq.explain: Assets are recorded at cost; later market rises are not recognised.

mcq.q: Providing for doubtful debts but not recording expected extra profit reflects
mcq.explain: Expected losses are provided for, anticipated profits are not recorded.

short.q: Why do accounting standards exist? Name the Indian bodies involved.
short.model_answer: Standards make financial statements comparable and reliable by prescribing common measurement and disclosure rules. In India the ICAI formulates and recommends standards, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs notifies them under the Companies Act, 2013, and NFRA monitors audit and compliance quality for larger companies. Ind AS, converged with IFRS, apply to listed companies and unlisted companies with net worth of 250 crore rupees or more; others follow AS.

common_mistakes: Mixing up accrual with cash basis. Accrual follows the event; cash follows the money.
Saying Ind AS apply to all companies. They apply only to those meeting the notified thresholds.
lessons.exam_tip: When asked to 'explain with example', give the concept in one line and a rupee example in the next. Examiners award the example.

lessons.title: The accounting equation and how transactions change it
objectives: State the accounting equation and its two forms
Analyse a transaction by its effect on assets, liabilities and capital
Show that the equation holds after every transaction

blocks.name: Accounting equation
blocks.note: Capital is what the owner has put in plus profits retained, minus drawings. It is also called owner's equity.

blocks.text: Everything the business owns (assets) is funded either by outsiders (liabilities) or by the owner (capital). That is why both sides always match. The equation is the reason double entry works: if a transaction touches one side, something else must change to keep the balance.

Transactions fall into a handful of patterns. Some swap one asset for another (cash for furniture). Some raise an asset and a liability together (goods on credit). Some raise an asset and capital (owner invests cash, or a sale earns a profit). Some reduce an asset and capital together (rent paid, drawings). Whatever the pattern, total assets remain equal to liabilities plus capital.

A profit does not arrive in a separate box. Selling goods that cost 60,000 for 90,000 raises assets by 30,000 net, and capital by the same 30,000. Profit is simply an increase in capital from operations.

worked_examples.title: Six transactions of Rohan Stationers
worked_examples.problem: Rohan starts a stationery shop and these things happen in the first month: (1) Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash as capital. (2) Buys furniture for 80,000 cash. (3) Buys goods worth 1,50,000 on credit from Sharma Traders. (4) Sells goods that cost 60,000 for 90,000 cash. (5) Pays shop rent 20,000 in cash. (6) Pays Sharma Traders 1,00,000. Show the position after each transaction.
solution_steps: After (1): Cash 5,00,000 = Capital 5,00,000.
After (2): Cash 4,20,000 + Furniture 80,000 = 5,00,000. One asset swapped for another.
After (4): Cash 5,10,000 + Furniture 80,000 + Stock 90,000 = 6,80,000. Capital rises by the profit of 30,000 to 5,30,000. Creditors 1,50,000 + Capital 5,30,000 = 6,80,000.
After (5): Cash falls to 4,90,000 and capital falls by the rent to 5,10,000. Assets 6,60,000 = Creditors 1,50,000 + Capital 5,10,000.
worked_examples.answer: Final position: Assets 5,60,000 = Creditors 50,000 + Capital 5,10,000.

mcq.q: If total assets are 8,00,000 and liabilities are 3,00,000, capital is
mcq.explain: Capital = Assets minus Liabilities = 8,00,000 - 3,00,000.

mcq.q: Purchasing goods on credit
mcq.explain: Stock (asset) and creditors (liability) both rise.

short.q: Mohan started a business with cash 2,00,000. He bought goods for 50,000 cash and sold half of them for 40,000 cash. State the assets and capital at the end.
short.model_answer: Cash after purchase 1,50,000; goods 50,000. Goods sold cost 25,000 for 40,000 so profit 15,000. Cash 1,90,000 + goods 25,000 = assets 2,15,000. Capital 2,00,000 + profit 15,000 = 2,15,000.

common_mistakes: Recording the full sale price as profit. Profit is selling price less cost.
Forgetting that drawings and expenses reduce capital.
lessons.exam_tip: In a transaction table, always write the new total of both sides after each line. If they differ, you have an error to find before moving on.

widgets.title: Watch the accounting equation hold, transaction by transaction

moves.text: Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash to start the stationery shop.
moves.why: Cash comes in, and the owner's claim on the business grows by the same amount.

moves.text: He buys furniture for 80,000 and pays cash.
moves.why: One asset swaps for another, so total assets do not move.

Cash and the amount owed both fall by 1,00,000.

lessons.title: Double entry, types of accounts and the accounting cycle
objectives: Explain the double-entry principle
Classify accounts and apply the rules of debit and credit
Outline the accounting cycle from voucher to financial statements

blocks.text: Double entry means each transaction is recorded twice: once as a debit in one account and once as a credit of an equal amount in another. Debit simply means the left side of an account and credit the right side. The words carry no moral meaning. They are a convention that lets the whole set of books be checked by a single test: total debits must equal total credits.

blocks.caption: Modern classification and rules of debit and credit

blocks.text: The traditional classification groups accounts as personal (people and firms: Sunil's account, bank account), real (assets and goods: cash, furniture) and nominal (income and expenses: rent, sales). Its rules are: debit the receiver and credit the giver for personal accounts; debit what comes in and credit what goes out for real accounts; debit all expenses and losses and credit all incomes and gains for nominal accounts. Both systems give the same answers. The modern approach is easier to carry into company accounts, so use it as your default and keep the traditional rules for exam questions that ask for them.

blocks.title: The accounting cycle
items: Collect source documents: invoices, bills, vouchers, bank statements
Journalise: record each transaction in the journal or a subsidiary book
Post to the ledger and balance each account
Prepare the unadjusted trial balance
Pass adjusting entries for items such as depreciation, outstanding and prepaid expenses
Prepare the adjusted trial balance
Prepare the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet
Pass closing entries and open the next period with the closing balances

blocks.text: A debit balance is not 'bad' and a credit balance is not 'good'. Cash with a debit balance is healthy. A bank with a credit balance means you are overdrawn.

worked_examples.title: Applying the rules to six transactions
worked_examples.problem: Identify the accounts affected and which side to debit and credit: (a) Started business with cash 1,00,000. (b) Bought furniture for 30,000 by cash. (c) Purchased goods from Anil on credit 40,000. (d) Sold goods for cash 25,000. (e) Paid salaries 8,000. (f) Received commission 5,000.
solution_steps: (a) Cash (asset up) Dr 1,00,000; Capital (capital up) Cr 1,00,000.
(b) Furniture (asset up) Dr 30,000; Cash (asset down) Cr 30,000.
(c) Purchases (expense of trading, up) Dr 40,000; Anil (liability up) Cr 40,000.
(d) Cash (asset up) Dr 25,000; Sales (income up) Cr 25,000.
(e) Salaries (expense up) Dr 8,000; Cash (asset down) Cr 8,000.
(f) Cash (asset up) Dr 5,000; Commission received (income up) Cr 5,000.
worked_examples.answer: Total debits = total credits = 2,08,000 across the six entries.

mcq.q: Which account is debited when rent is paid?
mcq.explain: Rent is an expense, which is debited when it increases. Cash is credited.

mcq.q: An increase in a liability is recorded by
mcq.explain: Liabilities increase on the credit side.

short.q: State the golden rules of accounting under the traditional approach.
short.model_answer: Personal account: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

common_mistakes: Debiting the giver in a personal account. Think who received the benefit.
Treating drawings as an expense. It is a reduction of capital and is not in the profit and loss account.
lessons.exam_tip: Before writing any entry, say the two accounts aloud: 'which two accounts, which is asset, liability, capital, expense or income, up or down?' The side follows automatically.

case_study.title: The tea stall that could not say if it made money
case_study.scenario: Savita runs a tea stall near a metro station in Delhi. She started 18 months ago with 40,000 of her own savings and 30,000 borrowed from a relative. She keeps her daily sales in a pocket diary, pays suppliers in cash, and uses the same cash box for stall money and household expenses. Last week a microfinance lender asked for her profit figure. She cannot give one.

questions.q: Which accounting concept is Savita breaking when she uses the same cash box for stall and household expenses? Explain the consequence.
answer_points: Business entity concept
Personal spending mixes with business, so profit is understated or overstated and the lender cannot trust any figure
Fix: separate cash box or bank account and record drawings explicitly

questions.q: Write the accounting equation for her business on the day she started.
answer_points: Assets (cash) 70,000 = Liabilities (loan) 30,000 + Capital 40,000

questions.q: Name the minimum set of records she should start to maintain and the reason for each.
answer_points: Cash book for receipts and payments
A simple sales register or daily summary for revenue
A purchases and expenses record for matching cost to income
A drawings register so household use is not treated as stall expense

mcq.explain: Money measurement limits recording to monetary facts.

mcq.q: A firm that switches depreciation method every year violates
mcq.explain: Methods should be applied consistently to allow comparison.

mcq.q: Assets 12,00,000; capital 7,00,000. Liabilities are
mcq.explain: Liabilities = Assets - Capital.

mcq.q: Which is a nominal account?
mcq.explain: Incomes and expenses are nominal accounts.

mcq.q: Ind AS apply to
options: Listed companies and unlisted companies meeting the notified net worth threshold
mcq.explain: Ind AS apply to companies meeting the thresholds in the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules.

mcq.explain: Drawings reduce the owner's capital; they are not an expense.

units.title: Recording Transactions, Trial Balance and Verification
units.summary: How a transaction travels from a voucher to the journal, the ledger and the trial balance, and what to do when the books do not agree with the bank or with themselves.

lessons.title: Journal and ledger
objectives: Pass journal entries with proper narration, including compound entries
Post journal entries to ledger accounts
Balance a ledger account and carry the balance down

blocks.text: The journal is the book of original entry. A transaction is first written there in date order, with the account to be debited, the account to be credited, the amount, and a short narration explaining it. Nothing is lost between a voucher and the books if every entry is made in the journal first.

A compound entry combines several debits or credits in one entry when they arise from one transaction, for example buying goods partly for cash and partly on credit. The only requirement is that total debits equal total credits.

The ledger is the book of final entry: a separate account for every person, asset, liability, income and expense. Posting means copying each journal line to the account named in it, on the same side. Once all postings are made, each account is totalled and balanced. The balance is the difference between the two sides, carried down to open the next period. A debit balance on an asset account means it is a resource of the business; a credit balance on a creditor account means money is owed.
In the ledger the 'To' and 'By' prefixes only point to the other account. Write the name of the other account on every line so that you can trace the entry in both books.

worked_examples.title: Journal and cash account for Rohan Stationers, April 2026
worked_examples.problem: Journalise and post the cash account: 1 Apr started business with cash 3,00,000; 2 Apr bought goods for cash 80,000; 5 Apr bought goods from Verma & Co on credit 60,000; 8 Apr sold goods for cash 50,000; 10 Apr sold goods to Gupta on credit 40,000; 15 Apr paid rent 10,000; 20 Apr received 25,000 from Gupta; 25 Apr paid 30,000 to Verma & Co.
solution_steps: 1 Apr: Cash Dr 3,00,000 / To Capital 3,00,000.
2 Apr: Purchases Dr 80,000 / To Cash 80,000.
5 Apr: Purchases Dr 60,000 / To Verma & Co 60,000.
8 Apr: Cash Dr 50,000 / To Sales 50,000.
10 Apr: Gupta Dr 40,000 / To Sales 40,000.
15 Apr: Rent Dr 10,000 / To Cash 10,000.
20 Apr: Cash Dr 25,000 / To Gupta 25,000.
25 Apr: Verma & Co Dr 30,000 / To Cash 30,000.
worked_examples.answer: Cash balance 2,55,000 Dr; Gupta owes 15,000; Rohan owes Verma & Co 30,000.

mcq.q: The journal is called the book of
mcq.explain: Transactions are first entered in the journal.

mcq.q: Goods bought for 10,000: 4,000 cash and 6,000 on credit from Ravi. The credit side of the compound entry shows
mcq.explain: Purchases are debited 10,000; Cash and Ravi are credited by their respective parts.

short.q: What is meant by 'posting' and 'balancing' of ledger accounts?
short.model_answer: Posting is transferring each journal entry to the debit and credit accounts named in it. Balancing is totalling both sides of an account, finding the difference and carrying it down as the opening balance for the next period. The balance shows whether the account is a debit or credit position.

common_mistakes: Skipping the narration. A journal entry without a reason cannot be audited.
Posting to the wrong side because the 'To' and 'By' words were confused.
lessons.exam_tip: Always journalise first, even if the question says 'prepare ledger accounts'. Examiners give marks for the journal as the working.

widgets.intro: Pick the account to debit and the account to credit for each transaction. Your ledger and trial balance build up as you post.

txns.text: Rohan brings 5,00,000 in cash as capital.
txns.why: Cash is an asset that increased, so debit it. Capital is what the business owes the owner and it increased, so credit it.

txns.text: Bought furniture for 80,000 and paid cash.
txns.why: Furniture (an asset) comes in, so debit it. Cash (an asset) goes out, so credit it.

txns.why: Purchases is an expense-type account that increased, so debit it. Sharma Traders is now owed money, a liability that increased, so credit it.
Cash comes in, so debit it. Sales is income, and income increases with a credit.

txns.why: Rent is an expense, and expenses increase with a debit. Cash goes out, so credit it.
The amount owed to Sharma Traders falls, and liabilities decrease with a debit. Cash goes out, so credit it.

lessons.title: Subsidiary books and the cash book
objectives: Explain why a business keeps subsidiary books
Prepare a three-column cash book with contra entries and discounts
Describe the imprest system of petty cash

blocks.text: Journalising every sale and purchase one line at a time is slow. Businesses therefore divide the journal into subsidiary books by type of transaction: purchases book (credit purchases of goods), sales book (credit sales), purchase returns book, sales returns book, bills receivable and bills payable books, the cash book, and the journal proper for everything else. Each book is totalled periodically and the totals are posted to the ledger.

blocks.caption: Subsidiary books at a glance
rows: Credit purchases of goods for resale
Each supplier credited, Purchases debited with the total
Each customer debited, Sales credited with the total
All cash and bank receipts and payments
Itself a ledger account for cash and bank

blocks.text: The cash book is both a book of original entry and a ledger account. A three-column cash book has debit and credit sides, each with columns for discount, cash and bank. Discount allowed (to debtors who pay early) sits on the debit side; discount received (from creditors we pay early) sits on the credit side. A contra entry is a transaction that touches both cash and bank, such as depositing cash in the bank; it is recorded once on each side of the cash book and needs no ledger posting.

Petty cash handles small day-to-day expenses. Under the imprest system the petty cashier is given a fixed sum (the imprest) for a period. At the end of the period the amount spent is reimbursed so the imprest is restored. Expenses are recorded in an analytical petty cash book with a column for each type of expense.
Many small Indian traders still record in a day book and bahi-khata. The same principles apply: record at the time of the transaction, keep a vouchers file, and balance the cash book every day.

worked_examples.title: Three-column cash book, June 2026
worked_examples.problem: Opening balances on 1 June: cash 25,000 and bank 1,00,000 (both debit). 3 Jun: received cheque from Rahul 19,500 in full settlement of 20,000 and deposited it. 6 Jun: paid Suresh by cheque 29,400 in full settlement of 30,000. 10 Jun: cash sales 15,000. 12 Jun: deposited cash in bank 10,000. 15 Jun: withdrew from bank for office use 5,000. 20 Jun: paid salaries in cash 12,000. Prepare the cash book and balance it.
solution_steps: Debit side: Balance b/d (cash 25,000, bank 1,00,000); Rahul (discount allowed 500, bank 19,500); Sales (cash 15,000); Cash (contra, bank 10,000); Bank (contra, cash 5,000).
Credit side: Suresh (discount received 600, bank 29,400); Bank (contra, cash 10,000); Salaries (cash 12,000); Cash (contra, bank 5,000).
Discount columns are not balanced. They are totalled and posted: discount allowed 500 to the debit of Discount Allowed A/c; discount received 600 to the credit of Discount Received A/c.
worked_examples.answer: Cash in hand 23,000 and bank balance 95,100 at the end of the month.

mcq.q: Depositing cash into the bank is a
mcq.explain: Both cash and bank are in the cash book, so it is recorded on both sides of the cash book.

mcq.q: Discount allowed is recorded on the
options: Credit side of the cash book
Debit side of the cash book
mcq.explain: Discount allowed to customers is an expense, shown on the debit side.

short.q: Explain the imprest system of petty cash with an example.
short.model_answer: The petty cashier receives a fixed advance, say 5,000, for the month. Small expenses are paid from it and recorded in the petty cash book. At month end the head cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent. If 4,200 was spent, 4,200 is reimbursed and the imprest is back to 5,000. It limits misuse and gives control over small expenses.

common_mistakes: Putting a contra entry on only one side of the cash book.
Balancing the discount columns. They are totalled only, because they are not cash or bank balances.
lessons.exam_tip: After you finish, check the cash and bank columns separately. Each should balance to a total that matches on both sides.

lessons.title: The trial balance
objectives: Prepare a trial balance from ledger balances
State what a trial balance proves and what it does not prove

blocks.text: A trial balance is a list of all ledger account balances on a given date, arranged as debits and credits. Because every transaction has equal debits and credits, the two columns should agree. If they do, the books are arithmetically accurate. If they do not, an error exists and must be found before final accounts are prepared.

blocks.title: Where each balance goes
items: Debit column: assets, expenses and losses, drawings, closing stock if given as an adjustment later
Credit column: capital, liabilities, incomes and gains, provisions

blocks.text: The trial balance does not prove that the books are right. It will still balance if a transaction is left out completely, if the wrong account is used, if the same wrong amount is entered on both sides, or if one error is offset by another of equal size and opposite direction. So a balanced trial balance is necessary, not sufficient.

If the trial balance does not agree, first check the difference. If it divides evenly by 9 the cause is often a transposition (for example 54 written as 45). If it equals a single ledger balance, that balance may have been left out.

worked_examples.title: Trial balance of Rohan Stationers at 30 April 2026
worked_examples.problem: Ledger balances: Capital 3,00,000; Cash 2,55,000; Purchases 1,40,000; Sales 90,000; Gupta (debtor) 15,000; Verma & Co (creditor) 30,000; Rent 10,000. Prepare the trial balance.
solution_steps: Debit balances: Cash 2,55,000; Purchases 1,40,000; Gupta 15,000; Rent 10,000. Total 4,20,000.
Credit balances: Capital 3,00,000; Sales 90,000; Verma & Co 30,000. Total 4,20,000.
Both columns agree, so the books are arithmetically accurate.
worked_examples.answer: Trial balance totals: 4,20,000 on each side.

mcq.q: An error of complete omission
options: Is revealed by the trial balance
Is not revealed by the trial balance
mcq.explain: Neither side is entered, so the totals still agree.

mcq.q: In a trial balance, drawings appear on the
mcq.explain: Drawings reduce capital and carry a debit balance.

short.q: List four errors that a trial balance cannot detect.
short.model_answer: Errors of complete omission, errors of commission such as posting to a wrong account of the same type, errors of principle such as treating capital expenditure as revenue, and compensating errors where one mistake cancels another.

common_mistakes: Putting a creditor's balance on the debit side because the word 'payment' appears in the question.
Forgetting to include opening balances.
lessons.exam_tip: Show a heading with the date, 'Trial balance as at 30 April 2026'. It is the standard presentation and costs nothing.

The book of accounts in which journal entries are classified under account heads.

lessons.title: Errors and their rectification
objectives: Classify accounting errors
Prepare rectifying journal entries
Use a suspense account to hold a trial balance difference

blocks.caption: Types of accounting errors
rows: A transaction is left out wholly or partly
Complete omission: no. Partial (one side only): yes
Wrong amount or wrong account of the same class
Wrong account: no. Wrong amount posted to one side: yes
Violating an accounting principle, for example capital item treated as revenue
Two or more errors that cancel each other

blocks.text: To correct an error, first decide what was done and what should have been done. Cancel the wrong effect and record the right one, using a single rectification entry. If the error affected one account only (a one-sided error), the other side of the entry is the suspense account. A suspense account is opened to hold the difference in the trial balance until its causes are found. Once all errors are rectified, the suspense balance should be nil.
Never adjust the suspense account just to make the trial balance agree and forget it. The difference is a symptom. Each rectified error must be traced to a source and recorded in the books.

worked_examples.title: Rectifying five errors with a suspense account
worked_examples.problem: The trial balance of Mehra Traders was short on the debit side and the difference was put to a Suspense A/c. Later these errors were found: (1) Purchase of goods from Mehta for 5,000 was omitted from the books. (2) Rent of 3,000 paid was debited to the landlord's personal account. (3) Furniture purchased for 12,000 was debited to Purchases. (4) The sales book was overcast by 1,000. (5) Cash of 2,500 received from Ajay was credited to Ajay but not entered in the cash book. Pass rectifying entries and show the Suspense Account.
solution_steps: (1) Complete omission, no suspense. Purchases Dr 5,000 / To Mehta 5,000.
(2) Wrong account (commission). Rent Dr 3,000 / To Landlord 3,000.
(3) Error of principle. Furniture Dr 12,000 / To Purchases 12,000.
(4) Sales overcast by 1,000 means Sales was credited 1,000 too much. This extra credit is why the suspense account was debited. Sales Dr 1,000 / To Suspense 1,000.
(5) Credit side only was done, so suspense was debited. Cash Dr 2,500 / To Suspense 2,500.
Suspense account: debit side opening balance 3,500 (1,000 + 2,500). Credit side rectification 1,000 + 2,500 = 3,500. Balance nil.
worked_examples.answer: Suspense account closes to nil; the original trial balance difference was 3,500.

mcq.q: Purchase of a machine debited to Purchases A/c is an error of
mcq.explain: A capital item was treated as revenue: error of principle.

mcq.q: A suspense account is opened when
options: The trial balance does not agree
mcq.explain: It temporarily holds the difference until errors are found.

short.q: Give the rectifying entry when goods sold to Kiran for 4,000 were wrongly debited to Kamal.
short.model_answer: Kiran Dr 4,000 / To Kamal 4,000. This removes the debit from Kamal's account and places it in Kiran's account.

common_mistakes: Reversing the sides in a rectification entry. Always ask what should have been debited and credited.
Putting the whole suspense difference into one account at the start without tracing causes.
lessons.exam_tip: Set out each error in three short lines: what was done, what should have been done, the rectifying entry. It prevents sign mistakes.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation statement
objectives: Explain why the cash book and the pass book bank balances differ
Prepare a bank reconciliation statement (BRS)
Handle an overdraft balance

blocks.text: The bank's own record of your account is the pass book (or bank statement). Your record is the bank column of the cash book. They should agree but rarely do on any given date because each side learns of some transactions later. A BRS is a statement that explains the difference. It is prepared to catch errors, detect fraud and confirm the true bank balance.

blocks.caption: Why the two balances differ
rows: Cheque issued but not yet presented
Cheque deposited but not yet credited
Bank charges, interest on loans, standing orders
Direct deposits by customers (NEFT, UPI, RTGS)
Interest or dividend collected by the bank

blocks.text: A reliable method has two steps. First, correct the cash book for items the bank knows and you do not (charges, direct credits, dishonoured cheques) to reach an adjusted cash book balance. Second, reconcile the adjusted balance to the pass book balance by timing differences: add cheques issued but not presented, deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited. Remember that these directions flip when the bank column is an overdraft.
When the balance is an overdraft the signs reverse. Always check at the end: does the reconciled figure match the figure you were asked to reach?

worked_examples.title: BRS starting from the cash book balance
worked_examples.problem: On 31 March 2026 the bank column of the cash book showed a debit balance of 85,000. A comparison with the pass book showed: cheques issued 12,000 not yet presented; cheques deposited 8,000 not yet credited; bank charges 500 shown only in the pass book; a customer's direct deposit of 6,000 shown only in the pass book. Prepare the BRS and find the pass book balance.
solution_steps: Cash book balance as given: 85,000 (Dr).
Deduct bank charges (not yet in cash book): 85,000 - 500 = 84,500.
Add direct deposit by customer: 84,500 + 6,000 = 90,500. This is the adjusted cash book balance.
Add cheques issued but not yet presented (the bank has not yet paid them): 90,500 + 12,000 = 1,02,500.
Deduct cheques deposited but not yet credited (the bank has not yet received them): 1,02,500 - 8,000 = 94,500.
worked_examples.answer: The pass book shows a balance of 94,500 at the bank.

mcq.q: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment are
options: Added to the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance
Deducted from the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance
mcq.explain: The bank has not yet paid them, so the pass book balance is higher than the cash book.

mcq.q: A bank charge shown only in the pass book requires
options: A cash book entry crediting the bank column
A cash book entry debiting the bank column
mcq.explain: The charge lowers your balance, so credit the bank column and debit Bank Charges.

short.q: State four reasons for a difference between the cash book and the pass book balance.
short.model_answer: Cheques issued but not presented; cheques deposited but not credited; bank charges or interest recorded only by the bank; direct deposits or collections by the bank not yet entered in the cash book. Errors in either record also cause differences.

common_mistakes: Applying the add and deduct directions for a credit balance when the cash book shows an overdraft.
Treating a BRS as a ledger account. It is a statement, not a double entry.
lessons.exam_tip: If the question gives the cash book balance, start from it and correct the cash book items first. If it gives the pass book balance, only timing items are needed.

case_study.title: The cheque that never cleared
case_study.scenario: Anjali Textiles in Surat issued five cheques worth 2,80,000 to suppliers at month end. Its cash book bank column shows a balance of 3,10,000. The bank statement shows 4,80,000. The owner suspects the bank has made an error. The accountant notes that two cheques worth 1,50,000 were deposited on the last day and are not on the statement, and that a customer paid 40,000 directly by NEFT, which is also not yet in the cash book.

answer_points: Cash book 3,10,000 + NEFT 40,000 = 3,50,000 adjusted cash book
Add cheques issued but not presented 2,80,000 = 6,30,000
Less cheques deposited not credited 1,50,000 = 4,80,000, which equals the bank statement
Conclusion: the bank has made no error; every rupee of the 1,70,000 gap is a timing difference or an unrecorded NEFT

questions.q: What actions should the owner take before blaming the bank?
answer_points: Check each cheque number issued against the statement
Check whether any deposits or charges appear only on the statement
Ask the bank for a ledger-level statement for the disputed amount
Introduce monthly BRS as a control

mcq.explain: Credit purchases are debited to the Purchases account.

mcq.q: The balance of a three-column cash book's discount column is
options: Carried down as the opening balance
mcq.explain: Discount columns are only totalled and posted to the discount accounts.

mcq.q: A trial balance will disagree if
options: Only one side of an entry is posted
A purchase is debited to Sales
mcq.explain: A one-sided posting breaks debit-credit equality.

mcq.q: Bank charges appear in the pass book but not in the cash book. In a BRS from the cash book balance, you
options: Add to the pass book balance
mcq.explain: Charges reduce the cash book balance when recorded.

mcq.q: A compensating error

Changes the totals of the trial balance
mcq.explain: Two errors cancel, so totals still agree, but both need correcting.

mcq.explain: Reimbursing exactly what was spent restores the imprest.

mcq.q: Goods returned by a customer are recorded in the
mcq.explain: Sales returns (returns inward) are recorded in the sales returns book.

mcq.q: A cheque deposited but not yet credited by the bank causes the pass book balance to be
mcq.explain: The cash book already shows the deposit; the pass book does not yet.

units.title: Depreciation, Inventory and Year-End Adjustments
coverage: Delhi University DSC (financial statements, earnings management)
units.summary: The adjustments that turn a trial balance into honest statements: spreading the cost of assets over their life, valuing unsold stock, and bringing in expenses and incomes that belong to the year but have not yet moved cash.

lessons.title: Capital and revenue items
objectives: Distinguish capital from revenue expenditure and receipts
Identify deferred revenue expenditure
Explain the effect of misclassification on profit and the balance sheet

blocks.text: Spending money does not automatically create an expense. If the benefit lasts beyond the current year, the spending is capital expenditure and is shown as an asset. If the benefit is used up within the year, it is revenue expenditure and is charged against income. The same distinction applies to receipts: sale of goods is a revenue receipt, while sale of a machine is a capital receipt.

blocks.caption: Capital vs revenue
rows: Purchase of machinery for the factory
Freight and installation to bring the machine into use
Cost of getting the asset ready for use
Repairs to keep the machine running
Major overhaul that extends life or capacity
Used up when goods are sold
Interest received on a bank deposit
Heavy advertising for a product launch spread over three years
Benefit extends over several periods; written off gradually

blocks.text: Misclassification distorts profit. Treating a capital item as revenue understates profit this year and overstates it in later years. Treating a revenue item as capital does the opposite and inflates profit and assets. Auditors watch this line closely.
Ask two questions. Does the benefit last more than one year? Does it add to or improve what the business can do? If yes to either, lean towards capital.

mcq.q: Wages paid for installing new machinery are
mcq.explain: Installation wages form part of the machine's cost.

mcq.q: Proceeds from selling a delivery van are
mcq.explain: Sale of a fixed asset is a capital receipt.

short.q: A trader spent 50,000 on repairing a machine and 2,00,000 on increasing its capacity. How should each be treated?
short.model_answer: The 50,000 repair maintains the machine, so it is revenue expenditure and debited to the profit and loss account. The 2,00,000 increases capacity, so it is capital expenditure and added to the cost of the machine.

common_mistakes: Treating all large amounts as capital. Size is not the test; benefit is.
Charging loose tools or small equipment as capital when the policy treats them as revenue because of materiality.
lessons.exam_tip: Write the reason in one clause beside each classification. Examiners award the reason, not just the label.

lessons.title: Depreciation: straight-line and written-down-value
objectives: Explain why depreciation is charged
Compute depreciation by the straight-line and written-down-value methods
Record depreciation, including part-year and disposal situations

blocks.text: The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life. It is a way of matching the cost of using an asset with the revenue it helps earn. It is not a fund of cash set aside for replacement.

blocks.title: Causes of depreciation
items: Wear and tear from use
Passage of time and expiry of legal rights, such as a lease or patent
Obsolescence, when new technology makes the asset out of date
Depletion of natural resources such as a mine

blocks.name: Straight-line method (SLM)
blocks.expression: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life in years
blocks.note: Equal charge every year. Often shown as a fixed percentage of cost.

blocks.name: Written-down-value method (WDV)
blocks.expression: Annual depreciation = Rate % x Book value at start of the year
blocks.note: Charge is higher in early years and falls each year. Book value never reaches zero.

blocks.text: Both methods are allowed for companies. Schedule II to the Companies Act, 2013 gives indicative useful lives and requires a company to justify different lives it chooses. For income tax the Income-tax Act has its own block-wise WDV rates that may differ from the accounting rate; this is why a business may show two depreciation figures. Depreciation is calculated from the date the asset is available for use. If an asset is bought or sold during the year, charge depreciation for the part of the year it was used.

Accounting entries: (1) Depreciation A/c Dr, To Asset A/c, or (2) when a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account is kept, Depreciation A/c Dr, To Provision for Depreciation A/c. At the year end the depreciation account is closed to the profit and loss account. The asset appears in the balance sheet at cost less accumulated depreciation, which is its book value.

Under the Companies Act, 2013 the amount of depreciation is based on useful life in Schedule II. Many small traders instead adopt the income-tax WDV rates in their books for simplicity; auditors accept this only when the rates do not distort the result materially.

worked_examples.title: SLM and WDV on the same machine
worked_examples.problem: A machine costing 5,00,000 was bought on 1 April 2023. Residual value 50,000, useful life 5 years. Calculate depreciation under (a) SLM and (b) WDV at 20% for the first three years, and show the book value at the end of each year.
solution_steps: Comparison: after three years SLM has written off 2,70,000, WDV 2,44,000. WDV is heavier in Year 1 (1,00,000 vs 90,000) and lighter by Year 3 (64,000 vs 90,000).

worked_examples.title: Part-year depreciation and sale at a loss
worked_examples.problem: A firm closes its books on 31 March. It bought a computer on 1 October 2025 for 60,000 and charges SLM depreciation at 25% on cost. On 31 March 2027 it sold the computer for 20,000. Calculate depreciation for 2025-26 and 2026-27 and the profit or loss on sale.
solution_steps: Year 2025-26: asset used 6 months. Depreciation = 60,000 x 25% x 6/12 = 7,500.
Sale price 20,000, so loss on sale = 37,500 - 20,000 = 17,500.
worked_examples.answer: Depreciation 7,500 and 15,000; loss on sale 17,500.

mcq.q: Under WDV the depreciation charge each year
mcq.explain: The rate is applied to a falling book value.

mcq.q: Cost 3,00,000, scrap 30,000, life 9 years. SLM annual depreciation is

short.q: Why is depreciation called a non-cash expense? Does charging it create a fund for replacing the asset?
short.model_answer: No cash leaves the business when depreciation is charged; the cash was spent when the asset was bought. Charging depreciation reduces profit but does not by itself set aside any cash. A replacement fund exists only if the business separately invests an equal amount.

common_mistakes: Applying the WDV rate to original cost every year; it is applied to the opening book value.
Forgetting to deduct residual value under SLM.
Charging a full year's depreciation on an asset bought a month before year end.
lessons.exam_tip: Present depreciation as a small table: year, opening value, depreciation, closing value. It makes checking easy and earns method marks even if one number slips.

widgets.intro: Change the machine's cost, scrap value, life or the WDV rate and watch how the two methods write the asset down.

outputs.label: WDV charge in year 2
outputs.hint: Lighter, because the base has shrunk

cards.back: Systematic allocation of the cost of an asset over its useful life.
Total depreciation charged on an asset since it was acquired.
Cost of an asset less accumulated depreciation.
Estimated value of an asset at the end of its useful life.
The period over which an asset is expected to be used.
Cost less accumulated depreciation; the book value on which WDV depreciation is charged.

lessons.title: Inventory valuation: FIFO and weighted average
objectives: Explain why closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value
Value closing stock and cost of goods sold by FIFO and weighted average
Explain the effect of the method on profit

blocks.text: Closing stock is the unsold goods at the end of the period. It is an asset in the balance sheet and it is subtracted from the cost of goods available so that only the cost of goods actually sold is matched with sales. Overstating closing stock raises this year's profit and lowers next year's by the same amount. That is why stock valuation is a classic route to profit manipulation.

blocks.name: Cost of goods sold
blocks.expression: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock
blocks.note: Carriage inwards and other costs of bringing goods to the shop are added to purchases.

blocks.text: Accounting standards (AS 2 and Ind AS 2) require inventories to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). NRV is the estimated selling price less the cost of completion and the cost needed to make the sale. This is conservatism at work: if goods will sell for less than they cost, the loss is recognised at once. For cost, the standards permit the FIFO (first in, first out) or weighted average cost formulas. LIFO is not permitted under Ind AS 2 and is not used in India.

blocks.caption: FIFO vs weighted average
rows: Every unit has the average cost
Higher closing stock, lower COGS, higher profit

worked_examples.title: FIFO and weighted average from the same data
worked_examples.problem: A trader's records for January: Opening stock 100 units at 50. 10 Jan purchased 200 units at 55. 20 Jan purchased 100 units at 60. During the month 250 units were sold. Calculate closing stock and cost of goods sold by (a) FIFO and (b) weighted average (periodic).
solution_steps: Closing stock units = 400 - 250 = 150.

(a) FIFO: the 150 closing units come from the latest purchases: 100 units at 60 + 50 units at 55 = 6,000 + 2,750 = 8,750. COGS = 22,000 - 8,750 = 13,250. Check: 100 x 50 + 150 x 55 = 5,000 + 8,250 = 13,250.
(b) Weighted average cost per unit = 22,000 / 400 = 55. Closing stock = 150 x 55 = 8,250. COGS = 250 x 55 = 13,750.
Difference: FIFO closing stock is 500 higher, so FIFO profit is 500 higher in a period of rising prices.
worked_examples.answer: FIFO: closing stock 8,750, COGS 13,250. Weighted average: closing stock 8,250, COGS 13,750.

worked_examples.title: Lower of cost and net realisable value
worked_examples.problem: At year end, 100 units of a product cost 400 each. They can be sold for 450 each but 60 per unit must be spent on packing and delivery. At what value should they appear in the balance sheet?
solution_steps: NRV per unit = 450 - 60 = 390.
Cost per unit = 400. NRV is lower, so value at NRV.
Closing stock value = 100 x 390 = 39,000 (against cost of 40,000). A loss of 1,000 is recognised now.
worked_examples.answer: Closing stock is shown at 39,000.

mcq.q: Under Ind AS 2 inventory is valued at
options: Lower of cost and net realisable value
mcq.explain: Inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV.

mcq.q: In a period of rising prices, FIFO gives
mcq.explain: Older, cheaper units go to COGS; recent, dearer units stay in closing stock.

short.q: Why does an overstated closing stock affect the next year's profit?
short.model_answer: The closing stock of this year becomes the opening stock of next year. If it is overstated, this year's COGS is too low and profit too high; next year's opening stock is too high, so next year's COGS is too high and profit too low. The error reverses over two years.

common_mistakes: Valuing stock at selling price. It must be at cost or NRV.
In FIFO, taking the closing stock from the oldest purchase instead of the newest.
lessons.exam_tip: Write 'Goods available' first (units and cost), then the closing units, then value the closing stock. COGS is the balancing figure and doubles as a check.

lessons.title: Adjusting entries: outstanding, prepaid, accrued, advance, bad debts and provisions
objectives: Apply the accrual concept to common year-end adjustments
Pass adjusting entries and show their effect on the accounts and the balance sheet
Compute bad debts and provision for doubtful debts

blocks.text: Cash moves on a different schedule from the events that cause it. Rent may be paid for 12 months in advance. Wages may be owed for the last week of March. Adjusting entries bring the books in line with the accrual concept so that each year bears the expenses that belong to it and earns the income that belongs to it.

blocks.caption: The four basic adjustments
columns: Where it shows in the balance sheet
rows: Paid but relates to the next year

blocks.text: Bad debts are amounts owed by customers that will never be collected; they are written off as an expense. A provision for doubtful debts is an estimate of future bad debts from the debtors still on the books. It is charged to the profit and loss account this year even though the loss has not yet happened, in line with prudence. The usual order is: first write off the further bad debts, then calculate the provision on the remaining debtors, then charge only the increase over the old provision (or credit the profit and loss account with the decrease).

blocks.name: Charge for provision
blocks.expression: New provision required - Old provision already in the books
blocks.note: A positive result is an additional charge; a negative result is a reduction credited to profit.

blocks.text: Do not charge the full new provision every year. Only the change in the provision runs through the profit and loss account. The rest is already there from earlier years.

worked_examples.title: Prepaid and outstanding expenses
worked_examples.problem: On 1 October 2025 a firm paid rent of 60,000 for twelve months. Salaries paid during the year ended 31 March 2026 were 1,20,000, and a further 15,000 for March is still unpaid. Show the rent and salary charge to the profit and loss account and the balance sheet items.
solution_steps: Rent: 12 months paid, 6 months (October to March) belong to this year. Expense = 60,000 x 6/12 = 30,000. Prepaid rent = 60,000 - 30,000 = 30,000 (current asset).
Salaries: expense = 1,20,000 paid + 15,000 outstanding = 1,35,000. Outstanding salaries 15,000 appear as a current liability.
worked_examples.answer: Rent 30,000 to P&L, prepaid 30,000; salaries 1,35,000 to P&L, outstanding 15,000.

worked_examples.title: Bad debts and provision for doubtful debts
worked_examples.problem: At 31 March 2026 sundry debtors were 1,00,000 before any adjustment. Bad debts of 4,000 are to be written off and a provision of 5% is to be kept on the remaining debtors. The provision for doubtful debts account already shows a credit balance of 3,000. Calculate the total charge to profit and loss.
solution_steps: Debtors after writing off bad debts = 1,00,000 - 4,000 = 96,000.
New provision required = 5% x 96,000 = 4,800.
Old provision = 3,000, so additional provision = 4,800 - 3,000 = 1,800.
Total charge to profit and loss = bad debts 4,000 + additional provision 1,800 = 5,800.
Balance sheet: debtors 96,000 less provision 4,800 = 91,200.
worked_examples.answer: Charge to P&L 5,800; debtors shown at 91,200 net.

mcq.q: Prepaid insurance is shown in the balance sheet as
mcq.explain: The firm has paid for a benefit still to come.

mcq.q: Old provision 6,000, new provision required 4,500. The profit and loss account is
mcq.explain: The provision is reduced by 1,500, which is a credit to profit.

short.q: Rent paid during the year was 48,000, which includes 12,000 paid in advance for next year. What is the rent expense and where does the 12,000 appear?
short.model_answer: Rent expense for the year is 48,000 - 12,000 = 36,000. The 12,000 is prepaid rent, a current asset in the balance sheet.

common_mistakes: Adding a prepaid expense instead of deducting it.
Calculating the provision on gross debtors instead of debtors after writing off bad debts.
Forgetting that every adjustment has a balance sheet effect too.
lessons.exam_tip: Every adjustment appears twice in the final accounts: once in the profit and loss account (or trading account) and once in the balance sheet. If you only entered it once, the balance sheet will not agree.

case_study.title: A good year on paper
case_study.scenario: Ranjan Auto Spares closed its books on 31 March 2026 with a profit of 2,40,000. The bank manager is reviewing a loan request. You find that: (1) the closing stock of 3,20,000 includes 40,000 of slow-moving parts likely to be sold at half cost; (2) debtors of 1,80,000 include 30,000 from a customer who has stopped replying; (3) electricity for March, 12,000, is unpaid and not recorded; (4) 24,000 spent on repainting the shop is capitalised as an asset.

questions.q: What adjustments should be made and what is the revised profit?
answer_points: Write stock down by 20,000 (40,000 x 50%) to NRV
Write off bad debt 30,000
Record outstanding electricity 12,000
Repainting is revenue expenditure: charge 24,000 to P&L, reduce the asset

answer_points: Conservatism and lower of cost and NRV
Prudence for bad debts
Accrual for the electricity
Capital vs revenue classification

coverage: Gurugram 241BBADSC2 Unit 2-3 (final accounts of non-corporate entities, non-profit organisations)

lessons.title: Trading account and profit and loss account
objectives: Explain the purpose of final accounts
Prepare a trading account and a profit and loss account
Calculate gross profit and net profit

blocks.text: Final accounts are the statements prepared after the trial balance and adjustments to show the result of operations for the year and the position at the year end. They have three parts: the trading account, the profit and loss account, and the balance sheet. Together they answer the two questions every owner asks: did we make a profit, and what do we own and owe?

The trading account shows the direct result of buying and selling goods. On the debit side go opening stock, purchases (less returns), wages and carriage inwards, and other direct expenses. On the credit side go net sales (sales less returns) and closing stock. The balancing figure is gross profit when credits exceed debits, or gross loss when debits exceed credits.

blocks.name: Gross profit
blocks.expression: Gross profit = Net sales + Closing stock - (Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses)
blocks.note: Equivalent to Net sales - Cost of goods sold.

blocks.text: The profit and loss account begins with gross profit on the credit side. It adds other incomes (commission, interest received) and deducts indirect expenses (salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation, bad debts). The balancing figure is net profit or net loss, which is transferred to the capital account. A sole proprietor does not pay himself a salary as an expense; his withdrawals are drawings, charged against capital.

blocks.caption: What goes where
rows: Opening stock, purchases less returns, wages, carriage inwards, other direct expenses
Selling, administrative and financial expenses, depreciation, bad debts, provisions
Gross profit, commission and interest received, other incomes

blocks.text: Closing stock shown as an adjustment goes in the trading account (credit) and in the balance sheet (asset). If it is already in the trial balance, it appears only in the balance sheet.

mcq.q: Carriage inwards is debited to the
mcq.explain: It is a direct cost of getting goods to the shop.

mcq.q: A sole proprietor's own salary is
options: An expense in the profit and loss account
mcq.explain: The business and the owner are one for tax; withdrawals reduce capital.

short.q: Why are sales returns deducted from sales in the trading account?
short.model_answer: Revenue is earned only on goods that customers keep. Returns reverse part of the sale, so net sales (sales minus returns) is the correct measure of revenue to match against cost of goods sold.

common_mistakes: Putting carriage outwards in the trading account. It is a selling expense and belongs in profit and loss.
Treating drawings as an expense.
lessons.exam_tip: Present the trading account and profit and loss account in vertical form too. Indian universities accept both; check which your paper prefers.

lessons.title: The balance sheet
objectives: Explain the purpose of the balance sheet
Classify assets and liabilities as current or non-current
Arrange a balance sheet in order of permanence and of liquidity

blocks.text: A balance sheet is a statement of assets, liabilities and capital at a particular date. It does not measure performance over a period; it is a photograph taken on one day. The accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) is the reason it must balance.

blocks.caption: Classification
rows: Held for long-term use, not for resale
Expected to be converted to cash within a year or the operating cycle
Stock, debtors, cash, bank, prepaid expenses
Creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft
Owner's investment plus profits retained, less drawings

blocks.text: Two arrangements are common. The order of permanence lists the least liquid assets first (land, machinery, then stock, debtors, cash) and the most permanent liabilities first (capital, then loans, then creditors). The order of liquidity does the opposite, starting with cash. Companies use a prescribed format in Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, which uses the current and non-current split.

blocks.name: Closing capital of a sole proprietor
blocks.expression: Closing capital = Opening capital + Net profit - Drawings (+ any additional capital introduced)
blocks.note: This is the figure that goes on the liability side of the balance sheet.

blocks.text: Show fixed assets at cost less accumulated depreciation, and debtors at gross value less the provision for doubtful debts. The net figures are what the balance sheet reports.

mcq.q: Under the order of liquidity, the first asset listed is
mcq.explain: Cash is the most liquid asset and comes first.

mcq.q: Bank overdraft is classified as
mcq.explain: An overdraft is repayable on demand.

short.q: Differentiate between a trial balance and a balance sheet.
short.model_answer: A trial balance lists all ledger balances on a date to test arithmetical accuracy; it includes expenses and incomes. A balance sheet lists only assets, liabilities and capital at a date and shows the financial position after adjustments and after transferring profit to capital.

common_mistakes: Setting outstanding expenses against the expense on the asset side. It is a liability.
Deducting drawings from profit in the profit and loss account instead of from capital.
lessons.exam_tip: Always cross-check: the balance sheet total of assets must equal the total of capital plus liabilities. If it does not, the error is in one of the adjustments or in the profit figure.

cards.back: A statement of assets, liabilities and capital on a given date.
An asset expected to be converted into cash within a year or the operating cycle.
An expense paid in advance that relates to a future period.
An amount set aside for an expected liability or loss whose exact amount is uncertain.
Cash or goods taken out of the business by the owner for personal use.
Trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet.
Net sales less cost of goods sold.

lessons.title: Final accounts with adjustments: a complete example
objectives: Prepare a trading account, a profit and loss account and a balance sheet from a trial balance with adjustments
Check that the balance sheet balances

blocks.text: This lesson works through a full question, the way a university paper sets it. Work through it with a pencil. The order that never fails is: (1) trading account, (2) profit and loss account, (3) balance sheet. For each adjustment ask where it appears: it normally affects one statement of results and the balance sheet.

blocks.title: A checklist for every final accounts question
items: Read all adjustments first and mark which account each one affects
Net the sales and purchases for returns before the trading account
Add outstanding and subtract prepaid expenses in the profit and loss account
Compute depreciation and the net provision for doubtful debts
Transfer net profit to capital and subtract drawings
Match the total of the two sides of the balance sheet

worked_examples.title: Meera Garments, year ended 31 March 2026
worked_examples.problem: Trial balance debits: Opening stock 80,000; Purchases 6,40,000; Sales returns 20,000; Wages 60,000; Carriage inwards 10,000; Salaries 1,20,000; Rent 48,000; Office expenses 36,000; Insurance 12,000; Debtors 1,50,000; Cash in hand 15,000; Cash at bank 1,25,000; Furniture 1,00,000; Machinery 2,00,000; Drawings 60,000; Bad debts 6,000; Advertising 24,000. Credits: Sales 11,60,000; Purchase returns 30,000; Creditors 1,10,000; Provision for doubtful debts 4,000; Commission received 12,000; Capital 3,90,000. Adjustments: (a) closing stock 95,000; (b) outstanding salaries 10,000; (c) prepaid insurance 3,000; (d) depreciate furniture 10% and machinery 15% (on the balances given); (e) write off further bad debts of 5,000 and keep the provision at 5% on the remaining debtors; (f) commission received in advance 2,000. Prepare the trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet.
solution_steps: Trading account debits: opening stock 80,000 + net purchases (6,40,000 - 30,000 = 6,10,000) + wages 60,000 + carriage inwards 10,000 = 7,60,000.
Trading account credits: net sales (11,60,000 - 20,000 = 11,40,000) + closing stock 95,000 = 12,35,000. Gross profit = 12,35,000 - 7,60,000 = 4,75,000.

Profit and loss debits: salaries 1,20,000 + outstanding 10,000 = 1,30,000; rent 48,000; office expenses 36,000; insurance 12,000 - 3,000 = 9,000; advertising 24,000; bad debts 6,000 + 5,000 = 11,000; additional provision (5% x (1,50,000 - 5,000) = 7,250, less existing 4,000) = 3,250; depreciation 10,000 + 30,000 = 40,000. Total = 3,01,250.
Profit and loss credits: gross profit 4,75,000 + commission (12,000 - 2,000 = 10,000) = 4,85,000. Net profit = 4,85,000 - 3,01,250 = 1,83,750.
Balance sheet liabilities: capital 5,13,750 + creditors 1,10,000 + outstanding salaries 10,000 + commission received in advance 2,000 = 6,35,750.

Balance sheet assets: closing stock 95,000 + debtors (1,45,000 - 7,250 = 1,37,750) + prepaid insurance 3,000 + cash 15,000 + bank 1,25,000 + furniture (1,00,000 - 10,000 = 90,000) + machinery (2,00,000 - 30,000 = 1,70,000) = 6,35,750.
worked_examples.answer: Gross profit 4,75,000; net profit 1,83,750; balance sheet total 6,35,750.

mcq.q: Net profit is transferred to
mcq.explain: For a sole proprietor, net profit increases capital.

mcq.q: If closing stock appears as an adjustment, it is entered
options: In the profit and loss account
In the trading account and in the balance sheet
mcq.explain: It appears on the credit side of trading and as a current asset.

short.q: Why does a balance sheet balance only after net profit is transferred to capital?
short.model_answer: Before the transfer, the trial balance carries incomes and expenses as separate nominal accounts. Closing them into the profit and loss account and transferring the net profit to capital brings the effect of all revenue transactions into the owner's capital, which restores the equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

common_mistakes: Applying depreciation to the net book value when the question says 'on the balances given'. Use the figures stated.
Putting the additional provision rather than the new provision in the profit and loss account.
lessons.exam_tip: Write the adjusted figure and its calculation beside each item (for example 'Insurance 12,000 - 3,000 = 9,000'). Marks are awarded for working.

lessons.title: Accounts of non-profit organisations
objectives: Explain how non-profit accounting differs from that of a trader
Prepare an income and expenditure account from a receipts and payments account
Prepare the balance sheet of a non-profit organisation

blocks.text: Clubs, societies, trusts and many NGOs exist to serve their members or a cause, not to make profit for owners. They do not usually keep full double-entry books for trading. At the year end they prepare three statements: a receipts and payments account, an income and expenditure account and a balance sheet. Donors, regulators and members read these same statements.

blocks.caption: The three statements
rows: A summary of the cash book for the year, opening balance to closing balance
Cash basis. Includes capital and revenue items, no adjustments
The equivalent of the profit and loss account; shows surplus or deficit
Accrual basis. Only revenue items of the year, with adjustments
Assets and liabilities at the year end
Accrual basis. The surplus is added to the general (capital) fund

blocks.text: Three points explain most of the work. First, capital receipts (such as a donation for a building fund, or an entrance fee the society treats as capital) and capital payments (such as buying equipment) do not go in the income and expenditure account; they go in the balance sheet. Second, subscriptions are an income of the year to which they relate, so they are adjusted for amounts outstanding and in advance. Third, the opposite of profit is called a surplus or deficit, and it is added to or deducted from the general fund (capital fund).

blocks.name: Income from subscriptions for the year
blocks.expression: Subscriptions received - Opening outstanding + Closing outstanding - Advance received for next year (+ opening advance if any)
blocks.note: Adjust for amounts relating to other years so that the income matches the year.

blocks.text: Registered Indian trusts and societies prepare statements in this format, and charitable trusts under the Income-tax Act are also expected to account for corpus funds separately. Donors often ask for the statement of income and expenditure along with the utilisation certificate for specific grants.

worked_examples.title: Green Park Sports Club, year ended 31 March 2026
worked_examples.problem: Receipts and payments account: Receipts - opening cash 40,000; subscriptions 2,10,000; donation for building fund 1,00,000; interest on investments 18,000. Payments - salaries 1,20,000; sports equipment purchased 60,000; electricity 24,000; printing and stationery 16,000. Additional information: subscriptions outstanding at the start 10,000 (received this year and included above); outstanding at the end 15,000; subscriptions received in advance at the end 6,000; salaries outstanding at the end 10,000. Sports equipment at the start was 2,00,000 and is to be depreciated at 10% on the total including additions. The investments of 1,80,000 are unchanged. Prepare the income and expenditure account and the balance sheet.
solution_steps: Subscription income = 2,10,000 - 10,000 (belongs to last year) + 15,000 (outstanding this year) - 6,000 (advance for next year) = 2,09,000.
Salaries expense = 1,20,000 + 10,000 outstanding = 1,30,000.
Depreciation on equipment = 10% x (2,00,000 + 60,000) = 26,000.

Income and expenditure: income = subscriptions 2,09,000 + interest 18,000 = 2,27,000. Expenditure = salaries 1,30,000 + electricity 24,000 + printing 16,000 + depreciation 26,000 = 1,96,000. Surplus = 31,000.
The building fund donation of 1,00,000 and the purchase of equipment are capital items. They do not enter the income and expenditure account.
Opening general fund = assets (cash 40,000 + subscriptions outstanding 10,000 + equipment 2,00,000 + investments 1,80,000 = 4,30,000) with no outside liabilities.

Closing balance sheet - liabilities: general fund (4,30,000 + 31,000 = 4,61,000), building fund 1,00,000, subscriptions in advance 6,000, outstanding salaries 10,000 = 5,77,000. Assets: cash 1,48,000, subscriptions outstanding 15,000, equipment (2,60,000 - 26,000 = 2,34,000), investments 1,80,000 = 5,77,000.
worked_examples.answer: Surplus 31,000; general fund 4,61,000; balance sheet total 5,77,000.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT recorded in the income and expenditure account?
mcq.explain: Purchase of a van is a capital payment.

mcq.q: The surplus of a non-profit organisation is added to the
mcq.explain: A surplus increases the general fund.

short.q: Distinguish the receipts and payments account from the income and expenditure account.
short.model_answer: The receipts and payments account is a summary of cash transactions that includes capital and revenue items and is not adjusted for outstanding or advance amounts. The income and expenditure account includes only revenue items of the year, on an accrual basis, and shows the surplus or deficit.

common_mistakes: Including donations for a specific fund or capital items in the income and expenditure account.
Forgetting to adjust subscriptions for opening and closing outstanding or advance.
Using the same figure for subscriptions in both statements without adjustment.
lessons.exam_tip: When a question gives only a receipts and payments account, compute subscription income with a one-line working before anything else. It prevents the most common error.

case_study.title: How a donor reads a small NGO's accounts
case_study.scenario: A school in Bhopal run by a registered society received a corporate donation of 5,00,000 to build a science lab. The society's accountant recorded the receipt in the income and expenditure account as income of the year. The year's other income was 12,00,000 and expenditure 11,20,000. The CSR officer of the donor company is reviewing the statements.

questions.q: What is the surplus as the accountant has shown it, and what should it be?
answer_points: Correct: the donation is a specific capital fund. Surplus = 12,00,000 - 11,20,000 = 80,000
The 5,00,000 belongs in a building or lab fund on the liabilities side until spent

questions.q: Why does the distinction matter to the donor?
answer_points: The donor needs proof the money is held for the stated purpose
Showing it as income overstates the society's operating surplus and hides restricted funds
Utilisation certificates for CSR funds depend on tracing the fund separately

Debited to the profit and loss account

mcq.explain: It is a summary of the cash book.
